questions.stem: In a typical soil profile, which horizon is the topsoil, rich in humus and biological activity?
options: The R horizon
The A horizon
The B horizon
The C horizon
questions.explanation: The A horizon is the topsoil, where organic matter mixes with mineral particles and most roots and soil organisms live. The C horizon is weathered parent material and R is unweathered bedrock.

questions.stem: The B horizon of a soil profile is often called the subsoil. What typically accumulates there?
options: Unweathered bedrock from which the soil formed
Most of the soil's earthworms and fine plant roots
Clay, iron and other materials washed down from above
Fresh leaf litter and partly decayed plant matter from above
questions.explanation: Water percolating down carries clay particles, iron and other substances out of the topsoil and deposits them in the B horizon. Leaf litter sits at the surface, and most roots and organisms are in the topsoil.

questions.stem: Which list gives the factors that control how a soil profile develops?
options: Clay, silt, sand, humus and the soil's water content
Parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time
Parent material, salinity, erosion, irrigation and fertiliser
Rainfall, wind, tides, sunlight and atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: Soil forms as parent rock is weathered under a particular climate, altered by living things, shaped by the slope of the land, over time. Sand, silt, clay and humus are components of the soil, not the factors forming it.

questions.stem: Two soils formed from the same granite. One, on a steep ridge, is thin and stony; the other, on gentle lower slopes, is deep. Which factor best explains the difference?
options: Topography, because erosion strips soil off steep slopes
Parent material, because the two granite bodies differ in age
Climate, because ridges always receive much less rain
Organisms, because ridges never support any vegetation
questions.explanation: With the same parent rock, the difference comes from slope: soil is washed off steep ground and collects on gentler lower slopes. The two sites share one granite, so parent material cannot explain it.

questions.stem: Two soils of the same age formed on the same rock type. The one in a warm, wet climate has a much deeper weathered profile than the one in a cold, dry climate. Which explanation is best?
options: Warm, wet climates deposit more wind-blown dust on top of the soil
Frost in cold climates breaks rock down faster than any other process
Warmth and moisture speed up chemical weathering and biological activity
Cold, dry conditions speed up the chemical weathering of the parent rock
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions run faster in warm conditions and need water, and warm, wet climates also support more organisms, so rock weathers into soil more quickly. Cold, dry conditions slow chemical weathering.

questions.stem: Which of these is a biological component of soil?
options: Earthworms, fungi and bacteria
Sand, silt and clay particles
Dissolved nitrate and phosphate
Air and water in the pore spaces
questions.explanation: Living organisms and their organic remains are the biological component. Mineral particles, air and water are physical components, and dissolved nutrients are part of the chemical component.

questions.stem: Humus improves soil quality because it:
options: Breaks down clay particles into sand-sized grains
Holds water and nutrients and improves soil structure
Raises the soil's salt content and also lowers its pH
Fills pore spaces so that air cannot reach the roots
questions.explanation: Humus is decomposed organic matter. It holds water and nutrients and binds particles into crumbs, which leaves pore spaces for air and drainage rather than filling them.

questions.stem: Which order lists soil particles from largest to smallest?
options: Clay, silt, sand
Sand, clay, silt
Sand, silt, clay
Silt, sand, clay
questions.explanation: Sand particles are the largest, silt particles are intermediate, and clay particles are the smallest, below 0.002 mm across.

questions.stem: Clay particles are defined as smaller than:
options: 0.2 mm
2.0 mm
questions.explanation: Particles below 0.002 mm (2 micrometres) are clay. Particles up to 2 mm are classed as sand at the coarse end, so 2 mm is the upper limit of sand, not of clay.

questions.stem: Using a standard soil texture triangle, a sample is 40% sand, 40% silt and 20% clay. What is its texture class?
options: Sandy clay
Silty clay
Sand
Loam
questions.explanation: Reading the three percentages on the triangle places this sample in the loam field, a balanced mix of particle sizes. A clay class needs far more than 20% clay, and a sand class needs well over 80% sand.

questions.stem: A texture triangle places a sample of 20% sand, 20% silt and 60% clay in a particular class. Which description of that soil is correct?
options: Loam, which drains and holds water evenly
Silt, which feels gritty and drains very quickly
Clay, which holds water well but drains slowly
Sand, which drains quickly but holds few nutrients
questions.explanation: At 60% clay the sample falls in the clay class. Tiny clay particles leave very small pores and a large surface area, so clay holds water and nutrients well but drains slowly and can become waterlogged.

questions.stem: Why does a sandy soil drain much faster than a clay soil?
options: Its large particles leave large pore spaces between them
Its small particles pack tightly together and so repel the water
Its particles have more surface area to hold water
It contains more humus, which channels water down
questions.explanation: Large sand grains leave large, connected pores that water drains through quickly. Clay's tiny particles have a huge total surface area that holds water, which is why clay drains slowly.

questions.stem: In a sedimentation test, soil is shaken in a jar of water and left to settle. Which layer forms at the bottom?
options: Sand, because the largest particles settle fastest
Clay, because the smallest particles are densest
Silt, because medium particles always sink first
Humus, because organic matter is the heaviest part
questions.explanation: Larger particles sink faster, so sand settles first, then silt, while clay can stay suspended for hours or days. Organic matter is light and often floats on top.

questions.stem: A 50.0 g sample of moist soil has a mass of 40.0 g after drying in an oven to constant mass. What is its moisture content as a percentage of the wet mass?
questions.explanation: Water lost = 50.0 - 40.0 = 10.0 g, and 10.0 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 20%. Dividing by the dry mass instead gives 25%, which is moisture as a percentage of dry mass, not wet mass.

questions.stem: A dry soil sample is heated strongly in a crucible and loses mass. Which component has mainly been removed?
options: Salt, which decomposes to chlorine
Organic matter, which burns off
Clay, which turns into a gas
Sand, which melts and evaporates
questions.explanation: Strong heating burns organic matter to carbon dioxide and water vapour, so the mass lost estimates the organic matter content. Mineral particles such as sand and clay remain in the crucible.

questions.stem: A few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid on a soil sample cause fizzing. What does this show?
options: The soil contains carbonates
The soil is strongly acidic
The soil is high in organic matter
The soil is highly saline
questions.explanation: Acid reacts with carbonates such as calcium carbonate to release carbon dioxide gas, which causes fizzing. Carbonate soils are alkaline, so fizzing indicates the opposite of an acidic soil.

questions.stem: Which measurement gives a quick estimate of the dissolved salts in a soil and water mixture?
options: Dissolved oxygen level
Electrical conductivity
pH of the mixture
Turbidity
questions.explanation: Dissolved salts form ions that carry an electric current, so higher electrical conductivity means more dissolved salt. pH measures acidity, not salt content.

questions.stem: A soil test gives a pH of 4.5. Which management response best suits growing most crops in this soil?
options: Adding lime to raise the pH towards neutral
Adding sulfur to lower the pH even further still
Adding salt to raise the dissolved solids
Adding sand to change the soil's texture
questions.explanation: A pH of 4.5 is strongly acidic, which limits the availability of many nutrients and can release toxic aluminium. Lime (calcium carbonate) neutralises acid and raises pH, whereas sulfur would make the soil more acidic.

questions.stem: A clay soil disperses and forms a hard surface crust when wet because a high proportion of its exchangeable ions are sodium. Which treatment is commonly used to improve it?
options: Applying sulfur dust
Applying gypsum
Applying common salt
Applying more water
questions.explanation: Such soils are called sodic. Gypsum (calcium sulfate) supplies calcium that replaces sodium on the clay, helping particles bind into stable crumbs. Adding salt would add even more sodium.

questions.stem: Children living near an old lead smelter have raised blood lead levels. Which exposure pathway from the soil is most likely?
options: Swallowing contaminated soil and dust from hands and toys
Breathing in lead gas given off from the soil surface
Absorbing lead through the skin while bathing in tap water
Drinking rainwater that dissolved lead from the clouds
questions.explanation: Lead in soil and household dust reaches children mainly through hand-to-mouth contact, and young children are especially vulnerable to its effects on brain development. Lead in soil does not escape as a gas.

questions.stem: Why can heavy metals such as cadmium in farm soil harm animals as well as plants?
options: They make the soil too salty for animals to drink from streams
They break down into nitrogen gas that grazing animals breathe in
They raise the soil's temperature until burrowing animals leave
Plants take them up and they pass to animals that eat the plants
questions.explanation: Heavy metals are not broken down, so plants absorb them and they move up food chains into grazing animals and people. Being elements, they cannot decompose into other gases such as nitrogen.

questions.stem: Soil at a former petrol station contains hydrocarbons, and a childcare centre is planned for the site. Which approach best protects human health?
options: Water the site heavily to wash the hydrocarbons into the stormwater drains
Grow vegetables for one season so the crops absorb all the contamination
Assess the contamination, then remediate or remove the soil before building
Lay turf over the site so that the children cannot see the contamination
questions.explanation: Contaminated land must be assessed and cleaned up to a standard suited to its new use before sensitive uses such as childcare. Washing contaminants into drains moves the problem to waterways, and food crops could pass contamination to people.

questions.stem: Which strategy best maintains soil as a resource on a cropping farm?
options: Retaining crop stubble and rotating crops to keep cover and organic matter
Burning stubble every year so that the paddock is clean for sowing
Ploughing repeatedly to break the soil into a fine, even powder
Growing the same crop each year so that fertiliser use stays simple
questions.explanation: Stubble protects the surface from erosion and adds organic matter, and crop rotation breaks pest and disease cycles and can restore nutrients. Burning and repeated ploughing expose and degrade the soil.

questions.stem: A farmer switches to no-till sowing. Erosion falls and soil organic carbon rises slightly, but more herbicide is now used to control weeds. Which evaluation is most balanced?
options: It fails, because any herbicide use destroys soil quality completely
It succeeds completely, because no-till has no environmental costs
It worsens the soil, because less ploughing always compacts the soil
It improves soil conservation but brings a trade-off that needs monitoring
questions.explanation: An effective evaluation weighs the measured benefits against the costs: less erosion and more organic carbon, against greater reliance on herbicides and the risk of herbicide resistance. Calling it a complete success ignores the trade-off.

questions.stem: What is primary soil salinity?
options: Salinity caused by spreading salt to de-ice mountain roads
Salinity that occurs naturally, such as around salt lakes
Salinity caused by clearing native vegetation for farming
Salinity caused by applying too much irrigation water
questions.explanation: Primary salinity arises from natural processes, as in salt lakes, salt pans and coastal marshes. Salinity caused by human activities such as clearing and irrigation is secondary salinity.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of secondary salinity?
options: Salt crusts that have long surrounded an inland salt lake
Salt marshes at an estuary that floods naturally with each tide
Salt left in coastal dunes by sea spray over thousands of years
Salt scalds appearing in a paddock after the native woodland was cleared
questions.explanation: Secondary salinity is caused by human changes to the land, such as clearing, that raise saline groundwater. Salt lakes, estuarine marshes and coastal dunes are natural, so they show primary salinity.

questions.stem: Why does clearing deep-rooted native vegetation lead to a rising water table?
options: Bare soil evaporates more water, so the deep groundwater rises
Shallow-rooted crops pump water up from deep aquifers
Cleared land receives more rain than land under forest
Plants use less water, so more rain recharges the groundwater
questions.explanation: Deep-rooted trees and shrubs use most of the rain that falls. Replacing them with shallow-rooted crops and pastures lets more water drain past the roots into the groundwater, so the water table rises and can bring salt with it.

questions.stem: In an irrigation area, more water is applied to paddocks than the crops can use. How does this cause salinity?
options: Excess water evaporates from leaves, leaving a crust of salt on each crop
The crops absorb the water and then release salt from their roots
The channels block groundwater flow, so rain can no longer reach the soil
Excess water raises the water table, bringing dissolved salt into the root zone
questions.explanation: Water that drains below the roots adds to the groundwater, so the water table rises and carries salts from deeper soil layers up to the root zone and surface. This is irrigation salinity, a form of secondary salinity.

questions.stem: Why does a shallow, saline water table cause salt to build up at the soil surface?
options: Salt crystals are lighter than water, so they float up through the soil
Plant roots pump salt up from the water table and drop it on the ground
Rainfall dissolves salt from the air and leaves it on the surface
Water rises through soil pores and evaporates, leaving the salt behind
questions.explanation: When the water table is close to the surface, water moves up through small soil pores by capillary action and evaporates. The dissolved salt cannot evaporate, so it is left behind and builds up as a crust or scald.

questions.stem: How can irrigation both reduce environmental water flows in a river and increase the river's salt load?
options: Water is pumped into aquifers, and salt is drawn out of the river into the ground
Water evaporates from channels, which cools the river and dilutes its salt
Water is diverted out of the river, and rising saline groundwater drains back into it
Water is added to the river, and it dissolves more salt from the river bed
questions.explanation: Diversions take water that would have flowed downstream, and over-irrigated land raises saline groundwater that seeps back into the river. Less water carrying more salt gives higher salinity, which harms wetlands and downstream users.

questions.stem: Students water bean seedlings with salt solutions of 0, 2, 4 and 8 g/L for three weeks and then measure their height. What is the dependent variable?
options: Seedling height
Salt concentration
Volume of water given
Type of seed used
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change, here the height of the seedlings. Salt concentration is the independent variable, and water volume and seed type should be controlled.

questions.stem: In the seedling experiment, mean heights after three weeks were 12 cm at 0 g/L, 11 cm at 2 g/L, 7 cm at 4 g/L and 2 cm at 8 g/L. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Growth rose as salinity rose, peaking at the 8 g/L level
Growth fell by the same amount at each step of salinity
Growth fell as salinity rose, with a sharp drop above 2 g/L
Growth was unaffected by salinity across the whole tested range
questions.explanation: Height dropped by only 1 cm from 0 to 2 g/L, then by 4 cm and 5 cm at the higher concentrations, so the effect becomes much stronger above 2 g/L. The decreases are not equal, so the relationship is not linear.

questions.stem: Why does salty soil reduce plant growth even when the soil is moist?
options: The salt raises the soil's temperature until the roots are damaged
The salt turns the soil water into a gas that roots cannot absorb
The salty soil water makes it harder for roots to take up water by osmosis
The salt blocks sunlight from reaching the leaves of the plant
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt lowers the water potential of the soil water, so water moves into roots less readily, or even out of them, by osmosis. Some ions, such as sodium and chloride, can also become toxic in plant tissue.

questions.stem: A landholder rehabilitates a salt-affected area by planting saltbush on the scald and deep-rooted trees on the higher land upslope where rain soaks into the groundwater. Why include the upslope trees?
options: They use water where it recharges the groundwater, lowering the water table
They shade the scald, so that less salt crystallises on the surface
They absorb salt from the air before it can settle on the paddock
They drop leaves that chemically neutralise the salt in the soil
questions.explanation: Treating the cause means reducing recharge: trees in recharge areas use more water, so less reaches the groundwater and the water table falls. Saltbush on the scald tolerates the salt and protects the surface, but does not fix the cause on its own.

questions.stem: Which land management practice most increases the risk of soil erosion?
options: Overgrazing that leaves the ground bare
Ploughing along the contour of a slope
Planting windbreaks along paddock edges
Keeping crop stubble on the soil surface
questions.explanation: Bare soil has no plant cover or roots to protect it from raindrop impact, run-off and wind. Contour ploughing, windbreaks and stubble retention are all practices that reduce erosion.

questions.stem: Why does ploughing up and down a slope cause more water erosion than ploughing along the contour?
options: Ploughing downhill leaves more stubble, which blocks the flow of the water
Ploughing along the contour exposes more of the bare soil to raindrops
Furrows channel run-off downhill, so the water speeds up and carries soil away
Furrows trap water on the slope, so the soil becomes waterlogged and slumps
questions.explanation: Downslope furrows act as channels, concentrating run-off so it gains speed and erosive power, which can start rills and gullies. Contour furrows run across the slope, slowing water and helping it soak in.

questions.stem: Which impact of soil erosion occurs away from the eroded paddock?
options: Loss of topsoil lowers crop yields in the eroded paddock
Gullies cut through the paddock and make it hard to work with machinery
Wind strips the fine particles that held most nutrients
Sediment makes rivers turbid and smothers aquatic habitats
questions.explanation: Eroded soil washed into waterways raises turbidity, blocks light and smothers habitats downstream, an off-site impact. Lost yields, gullies and nutrient loss are on-site impacts in the eroded paddock itself.

questions.stem: Soil eroded from farmland often carries phosphorus attached to its particles. What is a likely effect downstream?
options: Algal blooms, because the phosphorus enriches the water
Clearer water, because the particles settle out the algae
Higher dissolved oxygen, because the soil adds air to water
Lower salinity, because the phosphorus binds dissolved salt
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is a limiting nutrient for algae in many waterways, so eroded soil can trigger algal blooms as well as raising turbidity. Sediment makes water murkier, not clearer.

questions.stem: Students build three soil trays at the same slope: bare soil, soil with mulch, and soil with grass. They pour 1 L of water on each and collect the run-off. Which measurement best compares erosion?
options: Height of the grass in its tray at the end of the trial
Temperature of the run-off collected from each tray
Dry mass of sediment collected in the run-off from each tray
Volume of water that soaked into the soil surface in each tray
questions.explanation: Erosion is the removal of soil, so drying and weighing the sediment carried off in the run-off measures it directly. Water soaking in is related, but it does not measure how much soil was lost.

questions.stem: In the soil tray trial, the grass tray produced the least sediment. A student concludes that grass cover will prevent erosion on all farms. Which is the best evaluation?
options: The conclusion is valid, because the volume of water poured was controlled
The model used one small slope and soil, so the result needs testing in the field
The conclusion is valid, because three trays give enough repeated trials
The conclusion is invalid, because the mulch should have lost the least soil
questions.explanation: A small tray model with one soil type, slope and water volume cannot represent all farms, rainfall intensities and soils, so the claim overgeneralises. One tray per treatment is also not a repeated trial.
